Hi, this is Maya Okafor calling about my son Eli's class, he's in Mrs. Halvorsen's second grade room at Cedar Ridge Elementary.

I wanted to talk through something before I put it in writing, because I'm not totally sure yet what the right thing to ask for is. So, bear with me.

Eli has been running with me on weekends for about three months now. He's eight, and he's gotten way faster, and honestly he's gotten a lot more confident about it. Lately he's been asking if he can join the school's running club, the Cedar Ridge Cheetahs, which meets Tuesdays and Thursdays from three fifteen to four thirty. I think that's great, but the problem is that his after-school pickup has always been the aftercare program on those days, and I'd have to figure out a different arrangement.

I was thinking maybe I could just pick him up from the track at four thirty. Then I started wondering whether that's fair to the club coach, Mr. Dunleavy, because I'm not sure he'd want parents hanging around the fence every session. I could also ask whether Eli could stay in aftercare and get walked over to the track, but I don't know if the aftercare staff are allowed to do that, and I don't want to put them in a spot.

Okay, so, I think the cleanest version is actually this.

Could you let me know whether the aftercare office can release Eli directly to the running club coach on Tuesdays and Thursdays, with me listed as the pickup person at four thirty? If that's not allowed, then I'll just come get him myself, and I'll make sure I'm not late. Actually, I should be honest, I'm not sure I can make four thirty every single time, since I start a shift at five on Thursdays. So maybe it's better if I just sign him up for the club on Tuesdays only, and we keep Thursdays free. Hmm, but then he'll be disappointed, because he's really excited about both days.

Let me think about that for a second.

Eli's dad, Tomas, works later on Thursdays anyway, so he might be able to cover that day, but I'd need to check with him first. I don't want to commit to something on his behalf without asking.

So here's what I'd like.

First, could someone at the front office confirm whether the aftercare release to the club coach is possible? Second, if it is, could you send me the permission form for the club, and the schedule for the spring session, which I think starts on March ninth? Third, if it isn't possible, please let me know, and I'll figure out the Thursday question with Tomas.

You can reach me at this number, five five five, zero one four seven, or by email at maya dot okafor at mail dot example dot com. I'm usually free after eleven in the morning. Thanks so much for your time, and sorry for the long message.

I really appreciate it.

Hi Dana, it's Marcus Oyelaran from the design team.

I'm dictating this on my way into the office, so bear with me if it comes out a bit messy. I wanted to ask about the shared family calendar thing, the one HR set up for the flexible-schedule pilot back in March. I think it's a good idea in principle, I just haven't figured out whether it works for us.

So here's the situation.

My wife Priya and I both have kids, and our son Theo is in the after-school program at Maple Street Elementary until six. Priya's clinic has her on rotating shifts, so some weeks she's in at seven and some weeks she's not in until ten. The calendar is supposed to let us block off time and see each other's availability, and I've been trying to use it, but I'm not sure I'm using it right.

The main thing I'm stuck on is whether the calendar entries should be visible to the whole team or just to me and whoever I'm sharing with. I started out thinking it should be team-wide, because then people would know when I'm out for pickup and wouldn't schedule meetings at four fifteen on Tuesdays. But then I thought about it more, and honestly I don't love the idea of everyone seeing "Theo pickup" and "Priya shift" on my calendar. That's personal. Maybe I could just mark it as "Out of office, 4:00 to 6:00" without the reason, and that would be enough.

Actually, wait, I'm not sure that's enough either.

If I just say "out of office," people might assume I'm sick or something, and then I'd get weird questions. So maybe I label it "family commitment," which is vague but still tells people what they need to know. I think that's the middle ground. Or maybe I'm overthinking it and everyone already knows I have kids. Probably they do.

What I'd like to know is whether HR has a recommended setting for this, or whether there's a policy on what goes on the shared calendar. If there isn't one, I'd be happy to help write a short guideline, since I'm guessing I'm not the only parent wrestling with this. I could also talk to Tomasz on the platform team, since he set up the integration with the scheduling tool last quarter and might know whether the visibility settings can be changed per event.

Could we find fifteen minutes next week?

Thursday morning looks open on my end, around nine thirty, but I can move if that doesn't work for you. Let me know what suits.

Thanks, Dana.

Talk soon.

Talk soon.

I want to walk you through the brief for the talk, and I'll try to keep it in order, though I'll probably double back a couple of times because I'm thinking as I go.

So the event is the Northgate Systems Forum, which runs over two days in Leeds this year, the fourteenth and fifteenth of October. Our slot is on the second afternoon, 2:20 to 2:50, so thirty minutes including questions. Actually, let me check that. No, it's 2:20 to 2:40 for the talk itself, and then twenty minutes of Q&A, so you're looking at about twenty minutes of material, not thirty. That matters for how much you pack in.

The talk is called "Why Our Onboarding Dropped Off a Cliff, and What We Did About It." I know, it's a mouthful. The organisers liked it, so let's keep it. The audience will be mostly product managers and customer success leads, a few founders, maybe two hundred people in the room. They're not engineers, so cut the jargon wherever you can. If you need a technical term, explain it in one sentence and move on.

The core story is this.

Last spring, our activation rate, meaning the share of new accounts that complete their first real task within seven days, fell from around forty-one percent to just under twenty-six percent over about six weeks. Finish on what we'd do differently, which is mostly about monitoring funnel steps individually instead of only the headline number.

Slides are due to the organisers by Friday the twenty-sixth of September, so I need a first draft of the script by the nineteenth, and ideally a rough deck by the twenty-second. Keep the deck to about twelve slides. Use our standard template, which you should have from the shared drive under Brand, Presentations, 2024. If that link is broken, just ping Hannah in ops.

Budget is the agreed day rate for this kind of work, invoiced after delivery, and I'll send the purchase order number separately this afternoon. Let me know by Wednesday whether the timeline works for you. If it doesn't, tell me which part is tight and we'll sort it out.

Thanks again, Marcus.

Talk soon.

I'm pretty sure it's poison ivy, because I'd been pulling a lot of that vine out of the fence, but I'm not a doctor, and it's getting worse, not better.

I called on Monday morning, March 10th, and spoke with someone at the front desk whose name I didn't catch. She said she'd put a note in for a nurse callback within 24 hours. I did get a call back, but it was a voicemail on Tuesday afternoon, and when I called back it went straight to a full mailbox. I tried again Wednesday and was told the nurse line was closed for the day. Nobody has called me back since.

Then, this morning, I got an automated message through the patient portal saying my appointment on Thursday, March 13th at 10:30 had been canceled. I did not cancel it. I didn't ask for it to be canceled. I called the office again and the person on the phone told me the cancellation was probably a system error and that she'd "flag it," but she couldn't confirm whether I'm still booked. Thanks for reading this.

Dana Whitfield

Hey Marcus, it's Dana.

I'm dictating this on my phone from the parking lot at the Ridgeline trailhead, so forgive me if it comes out a little choppy. I just need to get this off my chest before I forget the details, and you're the one person who will actually understand why I'm irritated.

So, the group trip.

You know we booked the Halvorsen Basin loop for last Saturday, the fourteenth, with Priya, Tomás, and the two new guys from the Denver office, Callum and Ibrahim. I'd asked everyone to meet at the lot by six-thirty so we could be on trail by seven and get over the pass before the afternoon storms rolled in. The forecast had been clear about that. Storms after one, thirty percent chance before noon, and I put that in the group chat three separate times.

Callum showed up at seven-fifteen.

Ibrahim was at seven-forty, and he had not, I repeat not, brought a headlamp or a rain shell. He said he'd "figured it would be fine." Tomás had to give him his spare fleece, and Tomás is not a small guy, so the fleece was basically a tent on Ibrahim. I spent the first forty minutes of the hike doing a gear check I should not have had to do for adults.

Then there was the pace.

Priya and I had agreed on a steady two miles an hour up to the saddle, which is a reasonable clip for elevation gain like that. Callum decided he wanted to "push it" and took off ahead of us, and then he kept stopping every few hundred yards to take photos of the wildflowers and then waiting, shouting back that we were slow. We were not slow. We were on schedule. He just didn't want to hear it.

By the time we reached the saddle at eleven-thirty, the clouds were already stacking up over the ridge to the west. I made the call to take the short route down the Tamarack drainage instead of doing the full loop, and I wanted to shout at somebody when Callum argued about it for five minutes. Priya backed me up, thankfully, and Tomás just started walking, which was the right move. We were back at the lot by one-fifteen, and it started raining at one-forty. I'm not saying I was right about everything, but I was right about the timing.

Here's what I need from you.

Can you talk to Anders about getting a proper pre-trip briefing sheet for the Denver folks? Something with required gear, turnaround times, and the group rules, so I'm not the one playing bad cop every time. I'd also like us to agree that the group leader sets the pace, and anyone who wants to go faster can go ahead to the next checkpoint and wait there. That's not a punishment, it's just how we avoid splitting up on a mountain.

Okay, I'm going to go find a coffee before I drive back. I'll send the route notes and the photos I did get, the ones that aren't of Callum's flowers.

Thanks for listening to me vent.

Talk tomorrow.

Okafor from the Claims Processing team, and I'm dictating this because typing right now would be a disaster with how many times the app has eaten my words this week. I want to put something on record so it's not just me complaining in the break room. The speech recognition tool we rolled out on March 3rd, the one IT called "Scribe Pro," has been a serious problem for me and for at least three people on my team, and I need someone in HR to help push this to the right people.

Let me give you the specifics, because "it doesn't work" isn't useful to anyone. On Tuesday, March 11th, I dictated a claim denial letter for policyholder Renata Halvorsen, claim number CL-448-2217. The letter came out saying the denial was based on "a pre existing condition" when what I actually said was "a pre-existing exclusion in section four." That's not a typo. That's the software deciding it knew better than me, and in a letter like that it creates real liability for the company.

Please let me know by Friday, March 21st, whether someone can set up a call with IT and the vendor, and who I should expect to hear from.

Thanks for taking the time on this, Denise.

I appreciate it.

Marcus

The upstairs room holds about sixty people comfortably, and we've got twenty-two confirmed so far, so we're in good shape.

Thomas doesn't know about any of this yet, so please keep it quiet. His daughter Priya has agreed to bring him along on the pretext of collecting some paperwork from the hall office. She'll tell him at quarter to two that she needs a hand carrying things up the stairs, and that's when everyone should be in position. I'd ask that people arrive by one thirty at the latest, so we're not shuffling in while he's climbing the steps.

On food, I've asked Dimitri at the bakery on Harrow Road to do the cake. It's a lemon sponge with the blue icing Thomas likes, and he's collecting it himself on Friday afternoon. For savouries, we have Gloria Pennington covering sandwiches and sausage rolls, and Ahmed Farouk doing a tray of samosas. Could those two please confirm with me by Wednesday evening? I need numbers for the hall's catering list, which closes Thursday.

Drinks are simple.

Tea, coffee, and a jug of orange squash for the non-drinkers. Please don't bring extra bottles of anything alcoholic, because the hall rules don't allow it and I'd rather not have that conversation on the day.

Decorations and the banner are the responsibility of Kwame Osei.

If you have a memory of Thomas that you'd like read out, please write it down and give it to Priya before the fourteenth, or bring it on the day and hand it to me. Thank you all for pulling this together.

I'll send a written summary with the phone numbers and the timetable tonight, and I'll see you on the fourteenth.

Take care, everyone.

I wanted to walk you through what happened, what we've done since, and what happens next, so you have it in writing as well as in the voicemail I'm recording now.

The outage started at about 2:15 in the afternoon on Thursday the 14th of March. The utility company, Northline Energy, had a fault on the feeder line that supplies the industrial estate, and it affected roughly four hundred properties on that side of the road. Our site was one of them. Their crew confirmed the fault was on their side of the meter, so nothing inside your building caused it.

Your backup generator did not take over the way it should have. It started, but the automatic transfer switch didn't close within the expected window, so the server room lost power for about eleven minutes before the switch engaged. That's the part I'm least happy about, and I want to be clear that it's our responsibility to fix, not yours.

Since then, our electrician, Priya Shah, has been on site twice.

On Friday she tested the transfer switch under load and found a worn contact on the control relay. She replaced the relay on Friday afternoon, and on Monday morning we ran a full simulated outage from 8 a.m. to about 9:30. The generator took over in under six seconds both times, and the server room never dropped.

I also want to flag something we found during the checks.

The battery on the generator's starter was marginal, and given the age of the unit, we'd recommend replacing it along with the relay as a precaution. That's a small cost, and I've put it on a separate quote, which I'll send through with this email. You don't need to approve it today, but I'd like to schedule the work before the next maintenance window in April, so if you can let me know by the end of next week, that works best for us.

Going forward, I'd suggest two things.

First, we move the generator test from quarterly to monthly for the first six months, so we catch any problem like this early. Second, we give your facilities team a short written procedure for what to do if the generator doesn't start, including who to call and our emergency number, which is 0800 555 0142. I can have that document to you by Wednesday the 20th.

I know an eleven-minute gap is not something you wanted to deal with on a Thursday afternoon, and I appreciate you being patient while we got to the bottom of it. If you have questions, or want to go through the test results in more detail, call me directly on 0800 555 0167, or reply to this message. I'm happy to walk through it on site if that's more useful.

Thanks, Mrs. Okonkwo.

Speak soon.

Hey Dana, it's me, sorry, it's almost midnight and I'm sitting on the couch with the laptop balanced on a pillow, so if this comes out garbled just bear with me.

I've been thinking about the podcast idea we talked about at the Thursday standup, the one about the regional bakeries that are closing down, and I think I finally have a shape for it, so I want to get it down before I lose it, because I'm definitely going to forget half of it by morning.

The working title right now is "Last Batch," which I know is a little grim, but it's also kind of the point, and I'm not married to it so feel free to hate it. The basic premise is that we follow three bakeries across roughly six months, from the week they announce they're closing to the final day they open the doors, and we talk to the owners, the staff, and the regulars who come in every morning for the same loaf of rye.

So the first bakery is Halvorsen's on Pine Street, which has been open since 1974, and the owner, Gloria Halvorsen, told me on the phone last Tuesday that her hands hurt too much to knead anymore and her son in Phoenix doesn't want the business, and so she's just going to stop, and she said it in this really flat, matter-of-fact voice that honestly made me want to pull over the car. I think that's the emotional spine of the first episode, that flatness, the way people talk about the end of something they've already accepted.

The second one is a Vietnamese bakery over on Delancey called Bánh Mì Hà, run by a couple named Thi and Duc Nguyen, and their story is more about rent. Their landlord is selling the building to a developer, the lease ends March 31st, and they've been trying to negotiate for four months and I don't think it's going well. I haven't pinned down whether to actually record the landlord, which feels like a legal can of worms, so maybe we just talk to the couple and let the paperwork speak for itself.

The third is a kolache place in the Eastside Market, opened in 2009 by a guy named Ray Oduya, and I don't know much about his situation yet, which is sort of the point, because I want us to find out with him, not decide the story in advance. I'd like to set up the first interview with him for Saturday the 14th if he's free, and I already left him a voicemail, so fingers crossed.

Logistically I'm thinking eight episodes, about thirty to forty minutes each, and we'd need a recorder with decent wind protection because bakeries are loud and the ovens are right behind everyone's head. I can probably borrow the Zoom from Priyanka in audio, and I'll ask whether the studio on the fourth floor is free for the editing blocks in April.

Anyway, that's the whole thing, or at least the version I can hold in my head right now.

Tell me honestly if it's a dumb idea, and if it's not, let's grab coffee Monday morning and sketch out a rough outline before the Halvorsen closing date, which I think is May 2nd.

Okay, I'm going to go to bed now.

Talk tomorrow.

Best, Priya Raman

Hi, this is Marcus Delaney calling about my account, but actually I'm dictating this as an email so you can attach it to my file, so please pass it on to whoever handles complaints and billing for the garden services plan.

The account number is 4471-082-embers, no, sorry, that's wrong, it's 4471-082-6613, and the property is 17 Thornbury Close, Ashford, postcode AS4 9PL. Okay. Let me just get this down properly because I've got a lot to say and it's all kind of tumbling out.

So the situation is this.

On the fourteenth of March I signed up for the Greenline Garden Care plan, the premium one, which was one hundred and twenty-four pounds a month, and the sales rep, a woman called Priya Sandhu, told me it covered fortnightly mowing, hedge trimming twice a year, and a full autumn clear-up of leaves and debris from the back lawn and the side passage. I was really excited about it, honestly, because the garden had gone completely wild during the winter and I didn't have the time or the energy to deal with it myself, so I thought, brilliant, someone else sorts it out and I just pay.

The first visit was on the twenty-second of March and it was fine, the lawn looked decent. Then the second visit was on the fifth of April and they didn't do the hedges at all, they just said the hedge work was scheduled for later in the season, which I didn't know, nobody told me that, and it's not in the paperwork I got. Then I didn't hear anything until the nineteenth of April, when a different crew turned up, two lads in a van with no Greenline logo on it, and they mowed the front only and left a huge pile of cuttings all over the drive, and when I asked them about the back they said it wasn't on their sheet for that day.

I've now called four times.

Four times. The first call I got through to someone who said they'd log it, the second call was a voicemail that was full, the third call a man told me the back lawn was "out of scope for this route," which is ridiculous because it's literally in the contract I signed, and the fourth call, on the second of May, I was on hold for forty-one minutes and then it cut off. I've got the reference numbers written down somewhere, I think it's GL-88214 for the first one, and there's another one I can't find right now but I'll send it through if you need it.

What I'd really like is for someone to confirm the full schedule in writing, get the hedge trimming booked in properly for this month, and have the back lawn and side passage cleared, and I'd like a refund or a credit for the visits that didn't happen. I'm not sure exactly how much that is, I'd estimate roughly a third of the monthly fee for April, so around forty-one pounds, but I'd rather you work it out properly from your own records than take my word for it. Also, if there's a way to have one named contact rather than a different person every time, that would make my life so much easier, because I'm tired of explaining the whole thing from the beginning every single call.

I'm happy to be reached on my mobile, which is 07700 900214, or by email at marcus.delaney@mailbox.example, and I'm generally free after six in the evening or on Saturday mornings. Thanks so much for taking the time to read all this. I really do hope we can sort it out quickly, because I'd like to actually enjoy the garden this summer rather than feel stressed every time I look out the window.

Kind regards,

Marcus Delaney

Thanks so much, I really appreciate you sorting all this out.

Lily's already counting down the days, she's been telling everyone at the park about her new classroom, so we are very excited over here.

Cheers, Marcus Delaney

Hi everyone, it's me, sorry it's so late.

I'm sitting at the kitchen table with cold tea and I just wanted to get this out before I forget everything I meant to say, so bear with me. As most of you know, I applied for the community programs coordinator job at the Eastside Food Bank back in March, and I finally heard back this afternoon, and they want to interview me on Thursday the 14th at ten in the morning, so that's the news and I'm kind of freaking out a little.

The interview is at their office on Calder Street, the one above the old laundromat, and the panel is going to be three people: Denise Okafor, who runs the volunteer side, Marcus Bell from finance, and someone named Priya Nair who the email just described as the director of partnerships, which I had to look up, and I'm pretty sure she's the one who came to our spring drive last year and asked all those questions about the sorting shelves. So I'm hoping that helps a bit, because at least one of them has seen us work.

Now here's the thing I need from you all, and I hate asking, but the job posting asks for examples of leading a team through something messy, and honestly the best examples I have are all about this group. Remember the flooded pantry in October, when the pipe burst under the sink on a Saturday and we had to move four hundred pounds of canned goods into the church basement in about two hours? And the Halloween drive where we ran out of bags by eleven and Gerald somehow found a box of produce bags in his truck? Those are the stories. If anybody has notes, dates, photos, or even a rough memory of who did what, please send them to me by Tuesday night so I can pull it together before Thursday. Even a single sentence is great.

I also want to say, and I know this sounds sappy at this hour, that I couldn't have done any of this without you. Half of what I know about running a shift I learned from watching Lorraine fold crates at six in the morning, and the other half came from Tom yelling at the forklift, which I'm not going to recommend as a method. Whatever happens Thursday, I want you to know that this group made me feel like I could actually do something like this, and that counts for a lot.

Okay, logistics.

Saturday shift is still on as planned, same time, same place, and if you can't make it, let Gerald know, not me, because I'll be in a parking lot somewhere practicing my answers out loud and I won't have my phone. I'll report back Thursday afternoon, either way, whether I get the job or not. Thanks for putting up with me and my weird schedule, and for the many hours of coffee and sorting and laughing in the back room.

Okay, that's it, I'm going to bed now.

Goodnight, everybody, and thanks again.

input:
Hi everyone, it's Dana again.

I'm sending this from my phone because the power at the community center went out Tuesday night and it's still not back on as I'm typing, so I apologize in advance if this comes out a little scattered.

Here's what happened.

Around 7:40 on Tuesday, during the food pantry sorting shift, the lights just dropped and the whole building went dark. The breakers didn't trip, the fridges went quiet, and we lost about forty pounds of produce we'd already pulled for Thursday's distribution. Marcus tried to call the utility company from the parking lot and got an automated system that kept asking him to say his account number out loud. He said it four times. Four times! It didn't understand him once.

By Wednesday morning the outage map showed our block as "under investigation," which as far as I can tell means nobody has looked at it. Reggie drove over at lunch and saw a crew working two streets down, so at least we know they're aware the grid is out in this part of town. Nobody has told us an estimated restoration time, and the recorded line still says "we apologize for the inconvenience" every single time I call, which is not helpful when I have a walk-in freezer full of donated yogurt.

So here's where we are.

Thursday's distribution is moving to St. Brendan's basement, same time, ten a.m. Jamal has the keys and will meet people at the side door. If you can help carry tables over, please reply to me directly by Wednesday night so I know how many hands we have. Please don't come to the community center until I confirm the power is back, because the hallway lights are off and the back stairs are not safe in the dark.

I'll send another update tomorrow morning, or sooner if the utility finally gives us a real answer. Thanks for your patience, and thanks especially to Priya, who showed up with flashlights on her own before anybody asked her to.

Talk soon,

Dana

I am writing to confirm the brief for the online course we discussed, and to ask that you review it carefully before we proceed.

The course is titled "Foundations of Data Literacy for Municipal Staff." It is intended for employees of the Riverton City Council who work in housing, transport and parks, and it should take approximately six hours to complete, divided into five modules. Each module should open with a short video of no more than eight minutes, followed by a knowledge check of five to seven questions. The final module will include a practical assessment, which should be based on a real dataset that we will supply to you by Friday the fourteenth of March.

Regarding the tone and style, we would like the language to be clear and accessible, and free of technical jargon wherever possible. Where a technical term is unavoidable, please define it on first use. The council has asked that all examples reflect local conditions, so the case studies should draw on figures about Riverton's population, housing stock and bus routes. Mr. Dimitri Halvorsen, our communications lead, will send you the approved style guide and a set of brand assets by the end of this week.

Could you please send us a proposed outline and a timeline for production by Monday the twenty-fourth of March? We would then arrange a review meeting in the council offices at ten o'clock on Thursday the twenty-seventh. Your fee, as agreed, is four thousand two hundred pounds, payable in two instalments, the first on signature of the contract and the second on delivery of the final files.

If anything in this brief is unclear, or if you foresee any difficulty with the dates, please do let me know as soon as possible. I look forward to working with you on this project.

Kind regards, and thank you again for your time.

Sarah Whitfield, Learning and Development Manager, Riverton City Council.

Hi Margaret, it's Daniel here.

I wanted to follow up on our call last Tuesday about the renovation at 14 Alder Lane, and specifically the situation with the neighbour, Mr. Okonkwo at number 16. I know it's been a stressful few weeks, so I'll try to walk you through where things stand without making it sound more complicated than it is.

First, the good news.

Our crew finished the rear extension foundation on Friday the twelfth, which is actually two days ahead of schedule. The concrete pour went smoothly, and the inspector, Gerald Pike, signed off on the footings without any notes. So from a structural standpoint we're in really good shape.

The noise issue is the part I want to be upfront about. Mr. Okonkwo has called the council twice now, once on the ninth and again on the sixteenth, complaining about the start time on weekdays. He's asked us to hold off before eight, and honestly, that's a fair request. We were starting at seven-thirty because the concrete trucks were booked that early, and I should have checked with you before we agreed to that.

So here's what I've already done.

I spoke with the driver company yesterday, and they've agreed to move our delivery slots to eight-fifteen starting Monday the twenty-third. That means the mixing and the loudest equipment, the jackhammer and the saw, will only run after eight-thirty. I've also asked the crew to keep the radio off and to park the skip on the far side of the driveway so the lorries aren't idling right under his kitchen window.

I went round to see Mr. Okonkwo myself on Wednesday evening, and I'll be honest, he was a bit frosty at first. But once I showed him the revised schedule and told him he could call my mobile directly if anything goes past eight-thirty, he relaxed quite a bit. He actually asked whether we'd be doing the front fence next month, which I took as a small sign that we're getting back on decent terms.

Now, I do need a decision from you on one thing.

The revised delivery slots add roughly half a day to the overall timeline, and there's a small surcharge from the concrete supplier, about three hundred and forty pounds across the remaining pours. I think it's worth paying to keep the peace, but it's your budget, so I'd like your go-ahead before I confirm the change in writing. Could you let me know by Thursday the twenty-ninth if that works for you?

Last thing.

I'm going to send you a short written summary of the new hours and the complaint log today, so you have everything on paper for your records. If Mr. Okonkwo contacts the council again, having that log will make it much easier to show we responded quickly.

Thanks for being so patient with this one, Margaret.

I know it's not the most fun part of a project.

Give me a ring when you've had a chance to look at the figures, and we can talk it through.

Speak soon.

Mostly 8:45 to 9:15, but three nights it went past 10. Wake-up time is steady, around 6:30. So he's getting maybe nine and a half hours in bed, but not all of it asleep. That's the gap we need to close.

Night wakings: average of two per night.

Naps.

For the night wakings, don't go in right away.

Give him about three minutes, see if he settles. If he doesn't, go in, keep it brief, no conversation, no turning on the big light. Quiet, boring, same thing every time. I'll put a short script in the handout so whoever's on nights is on the same page.

I did receive your automated shipping notice on the twenty-sixth, which listed a tracking number ending in 7731. When I checked that tracking number with the carrier, it showed the package had been held at the Dayton distribution center since the twenty-fourth, with no further updates. I'd be grateful if you could look into that hold and let me know whether the shipment is still in your possession or has been released.

Our production line is scheduled to start the assembly run on the third of April, so we need these brackets in hand by the end of this week to keep that date. If the shipment can't be delivered by Friday the thirty-first, could you please let me know as soon as possible so we can decide whether to arrange a partial delivery or move the run back a week? Hi Priya, it's me again.

Thanks for getting back to me so quickly yesterday, I really appreciate it. I wanted to walk you through the brief for the enrolment form properly, because I think the last version I sent over was missing a lot, and honestly I'm a bit frustrated with how the whole thing has gone so far.

So here's the situation.

Our school, Westbrook Community Primary, is changing how we collect enrolment details for the autumn intake. Right now parents fill in a paper form at the front office, and the office staff, Denise and Marcus, spend about three hours a day re-typing everything into the admin system. That's the problem we're trying to solve. We want a fillable web form that parents can complete from their phones, and the data should go straight into the system without anyone re-keying it.

Now, the part I keep coming back to is the deadline.

The board has signed off on the budget, but they need a working prototype by Friday the 14th of March, not the 28th like I originally said. I know, I know, that's my mistake, I misread the timeline in the email from Gerald in governance. So I'm sorry for the scramble, but we really do need something testable by then, even if it's rough around the edges.

Let me list what the form has to do, because I don't want any more back and forth. First, it needs to handle two guardians per child, with separate contact details for each. Second, there's a section for medical conditions and allergies, and that section has to be mandatory, no skipping it. Third, we need a document upload for proof of address, accepting PDF, JPG and PNG, with a size limit of ten megabytes. Fourth, the form has to save progress, because a lot of parents will start it on their phone during a lunch break and finish later. And fifth, it needs to be accessible, meeting WCAG 2.1 AA, since the council audits us on that.

On the design side, please keep it simple.

The school colours are navy and gold, and I'd like the logo top left on every page. I don't want a fancy multi-step animation thing. Denise specifically said parents get confused when the page jumps around, so keep the layout stable.

For the handover, I need the source files, a short setup guide for Marcus so he can update the dropdown options himself, and a note on where the data is stored. Parents will be giving us children's health information, so I need to be sure it's held in the UK and encrypted both in transit and at rest. If that isn't possible with the platform you're proposing, tell me now, not in two weeks.

Can you send me a revised quote and a timeline by Wednesday the 5th? I'd like to see it before the governors' meeting on the 7th. If the price has gone up because of the earlier date, just say so plainly and we'll sort it out.

Sorry this email is so long and a bit grumpy.

I'm not cross with you, I'm cross with the timeline.

Anyway, thanks again, and speak soon.

Hi everyone, it's Marisol here.

I wanted to send this out before Thursday's meeting so you have a bit of time to think about it, and because a few of you asked me last month how we're doing with the grocery budget for the Eastside Food Pantry. So here's the honest picture.

We started the year with a budget of forty-two hundred dollars for purchased food, which covers the things we can't get from the regional food bank, like milk, eggs, cooking oil, and the fresh produce we pick up from Greenleaf Market on Tuesdays. Through the end of March we've spent about thirty-one hundred of that. On paper that sounds fine, but we're running about eleven percent faster than last year, and the reason is mostly milk and eggs. Prices went up again in February, and we've been buying more of both because the families coming in on Saturdays have asked for them specifically.

I don't want anyone to panic.

We're not in trouble. But I do think we need to make a couple of decisions together, and that's why I'm writing.

The first question is about the Tuesday produce run.

Dariusz has been driving the van to Greenleaf every week, and it's become a real chunk of our time and gas money. Greenleaf offered us a standing donation of day-old bakery and produce if we can pick up on Thursday afternoons instead, starting April 10th. Dariusz says he can do Thursdays, but he'd need one more person on the rotation, so if you have a free Thursday between two and five and a working car, please let me know.

The second question is whether we should cap how much milk and eggs each household gets per visit. I know that's a sensitive thing to talk about. Nobody wants to tell a family they can't have what they need. My thinking is that we keep it generous, maybe two gallons of milk and one dozen eggs per household, and then use the savings to buy more shelf-stable protein like canned beans and peanut butter, which people also say they need. Ruth raised this idea and she's got some numbers she put together on the spreadsheet in the shared folder, so take a look before Thursday if you can.

Thursday's meeting is at the church basement on Maple Street, six-thirty, same as always. Bring coffee if you're the one who usually brings coffee, because Pete says we're down to the cheap stuff again.

Thanks, all of you.

You make this work, and I'm grateful every single week.

Talk soon,

Marisol

I started back in March, right after the Lisbon offsite got moved to September. Mira from the Porto team suggested I might want to be able to hold a basic conversation before we visit, and I thought, sure, how hard can it be. Turns out it's harder than I expected, mostly because the pronunciation is so far from what I know from Spanish. Everyone said they're similar, and they are, in the spelling, but when people actually talk it's like a completely different sound system.

I've been doing forty minutes a day on an app, plus a tutor on Tuesday and Thursday evenings. Her name is Inês, she's really patient, and she's the one who told me I was over-relying on the app's translation tiles. I think she's right. I've been reading the sentences in English in my head first and then converting them, which is slow and kind of fights the whole point.

So I was going to ask you something.

I'm wondering whether I should switch to a more intensive course, like the three-week immersion in Coimbra that starts on the fourteenth of October. It's expensive, around twenty-two hundred euros with accommodation, and I'm not sure the company would cover it. I could ask Priya in finance, but honestly I'm not sure I want to put in that request yet. Part of me thinks I should just keep going with Inês and see how I feel in another couple of months.

Hmm.

Actually, let me think about this a bit more out loud, because I keep going back and forth. The immersion would make the biggest difference, I'm fairly sure of that. No, wait.

I think I was overcomplicating it. The review is on the twentieth, so the course would only overlap with the first week of it, and I could move my slides forward. So maybe the timing isn't the problem after all. The real question is just whether the money is worth it, and whether I'd actually use the Portuguese on this project.

You've worked with the Porto team longer than I have. Do they mostly speak English in meetings, or is it going to matter if I can follow a conversation in Portuguese? If it's mostly English, I might be better off putting the budget toward a few lessons with Inês and saving the immersion for next year.

Thanks, I really appreciate it.

Okay, that's my train stop coming up, so I'll stop there.

Speak soon.

Hi Mrs. Delgado, this is Rachel Okafor, Mateo's mom.

I'm dictating this on my phone in the car because I've been trying to type it for twenty minutes and the keyboard keeps eating my words, so forgive me if it reads a little strange. I'm writing about the reading app the school asked us to set up for Mateo's homework, the one called ReadRight Junior.

Let me start with what happened on Tuesday, March 11th.

Mateo had his reading log due Wednesday, and he spent almost forty minutes reading the same paragraph out loud to the app about a bear who goes to the market. Every time he said "market," it wrote down "mark it." Every single time. He tried saying it slower, he tried saying it louder, and finally he just put his head down on the table and said, "It doesn't like me." That broke my heart a little, honestly.

So I went through the settings.

There's a pronunciation setting, but it only lets you adjust the speed, not the accent or the dialect, and the app doesn't seem to know that a lot of kids in our house say words a little differently than the recordings it was trained on. Mateo's grandmother lives with us, and he picks up a lot of her phrasing. I'm not blaming him or her. I'm saying the app assumes one kind of voice, and it isn't built for a seven-year-old who's still learning how sounds fit together.

I also called the company's support line on Thursday, March 13th, and waited on hold for thirty-two minutes. The person I reached, a man named Derek, was nice, but he told me the feature works best in a quiet room with a headset microphone. We don't own a headset. We own one tablet and a kitchen where the dishwasher runs at the same time as everything else. He suggested I "try a different room," which is not a real answer when the homework is supposed to be done on the living room couch.

I'd also like to know whether other families have run into this with ReadRight, so I don't feel like the only person whose kid is being told "mark it" when he means market. If the school has a headset it can lend out, I'd take that too, but I'd rather not make that our problem to solve.

I know you're busy, and I don't want this to land on you as a complaint about your staff, because you've been wonderful with him this year. I just need someone to tell me what the plan is before the next reading log is due on Monday, March 17th.

Thank you for reading this, even in its messy, dictated form.

You can reach me at this number or at rokafor@mailbox.example, whichever is faster for you.

Best,

Rachel Okafor

Hi Priya, this is Daniel Okafor from the design team, calling to follow up on the photo archive backup plan I mentioned at Monday's team meeting.

I've put some thought into it over the last couple of weeks, so I'd like to walk you through it properly and then send the written version over to you.

The problem is simple to describe.

Our team holds about four terabytes of client photography, most of it from the Harbourview and Eastline shoots in 2022 and 2023, and right now it lives on a single network drive in the studio cupboard. If that drive fails, or if someone accidentally deletes a project folder, we don't have a reliable way to get it back. That's the risk I want to close.

My proposal has three parts.

The first is a local copy. I'd like to move the full archive onto a second network storage unit, a two-bay device with mirrored disks, which Tomasz in IT has already priced at about eight hundred and forty pounds. That gives us protection against a single disk failing, which is the most common cause of trouble with drives like this.

The second part is an offsite copy.

I'd use a cloud storage service with a flat monthly fee for archival storage, rather than the consumer plan we currently pay for. I've compared three providers, and the one I'd recommend is Brightwater Archive, mainly because it keeps files in two UK data centres and allows us to set deletion protection, so nobody can permanently remove a folder by mistake for thirty days. The estimated cost is around ninety-five pounds a month for the first year.

The third part is the schedule.

I suggest a full sync to the offsite copy every Friday evening, and an incremental sync every night for active projects only. I'd also like to run a restore test once a quarter. The first one I'd suggest for the second Thursday of March, pulling a single project folder back from the cloud copy and confirming it opens properly. A backup we've never restored from is really just a hope, so I think the test matters as much as the copying.

On responsibilities, I'd be happy to own the setup and the monthly check, with Tomasz handling the hardware and the account admin. I'd like Sarah Mensah in operations to sign off on the budget, since this is a recurring cost and it should sit in the studio's running expenses rather than my project budget.

If you're comfortable with this, the next step would be a short meeting in the week of the twentieth, so we can confirm the spend and pick a start date. I'll send a written summary this afternoon with the quotes attached, and I'm around all week if you'd rather talk it through first.

Thanks, Priya.

I appreciate you making time for this.

Speak soon.

Hi Priya, thanks for picking this up while I'm out.

I'm going to walk you through the enrolment form for the Hollowmere Primary admissions round, because there are a few things that trip people up every year and I'd rather you hear them from me than find them the hard way.

First, the form itself.

It's the blue two-page version, not the green one from last year. The green one was retired at the start of March, and the school office has been returning them without processing, so if any families send the old version, please ask them to resubmit on the new one. The new form is on the shared drive under Admissions, in the folder called 2025 Intake.

Second, the deadline.

Applications close on Friday the fourteenth of March at five in the afternoon. That's a hard cutoff for the portal, and the portal locks automatically, so there's no grace period. I'd suggest we send a reminder to the three families we haven't heard back from by Wednesday morning, just so nobody is scrambling on the Friday.

Third, the proof of address.

This is where most of the queries come from. We need two documents dated within the last three months, and they need to show the parent's name and the home address exactly as it appears on the enrolment form. A council tax letter counts. A mobile phone bill usually doesn't, unless it's a landline or broadband bill with a physical address printed on it. If someone brings a tenancy agreement, it has to be signed and include the start date. I've attached a one-page checklist I put together last term, which you can forward directly to families. It lists the acceptable documents with examples.

Fourth, the medical section.

Section C asks about allergies and medication, and the box is easy to skip because it sits at the bottom of page two. If a family leaves it blank, the office will call them, which slows everything down. If the answer is none, they should still tick the box that says none. I've had two cases already this week where the field was left empty and it caused a delay of several days.

Fifth, the sibling declaration.

If the child has a brother or sister already at Hollowmere, the family needs to tick section E and give the sibling's full name and year group. This matters because siblings get priority placement under the oversubscription criteria, and if the box isn't ticked, the application gets scored as a standard one. We've had that happen twice, and both families were upset when they found out afterwards.

Last thing, the signature.

Both parents or guardians with parental responsibility need to sign, or the form has to include a note explaining why only one signature is provided. A single signature without a note goes back to the family. Dr. Okonkwo in the office has the list of which families are single-guardian cases, so check with her before you send anything back.

If you get stuck on anything, Dr. Okonkwo is the person to ask, and she's in every day until half past three. Otherwise, I'll be back on Monday the tenth and can pick up anything left over then.

Thanks again for covering this.

I really appreciate it.

Thanks, Priya.

Hi everyone, it's Marisol here.

I wanted to send this out to the whole Riverside Community Garden crew instead of trying to explain it at Saturday's work day, because I think it'll be easier for people to read it once and then reply. So, the thing is, we've been talking about switching how we log the seed swap and the tool library sign-outs, and I've been testing a speech recognition app that might make that a lot less painful.

Here's what happened.

Last Tuesday, June 11th, I was standing in the shed with a clipboard in one hand and a trowel in the other, trying to write down who took the long-handled loppers, and I thought, why am I doing this by hand? So I opened the app on my phone, a free one called Scribbly, and just talked. I said, "Dana borrowed the loppers at 9:40, returned them at 11:15, condition good, one blade a little dull." And it got almost all of it right. It put the times in correctly, it spelled Dana without me having to spell it, and it even figured out that "blade a little dull" was a note and not a name. Honestly I was pretty impressed.

It did trip up on a couple of things, though.

It wrote "Hollis" as "Holly's," which, fine, that's a typo waiting to happen. And when I said "bed seven," it gave me "bed 7" but then "bed seven" again two lines later. So you still have to look it over. I wouldn't trust it blindly, especially for anything we'd use to settle a argument about who owes us a shovel.

Anyway, what I'm proposing is that we run a two-week trial starting Monday, June 17th. Anyone who wants to can use the app for tool sign-outs, and we'll compare the results against the paper sheet. Ibrahim has offered to set up a shared folder where the exported notes go, so nothing gets lost in someone's phone.

Reply to me or grab me Saturday if you're interested.

If you'd rather stick with paper, that's totally fine too. Thanks, all.

Marisol
